What do my files get reused for when I recycle them?

When you delete a file it's not actually deleted. At the most basic level on your hard disk you basically have a telephone book known as a File Allocation Table (think the FAT in file systems like FAT32) that indicates where files are stored. This is complex as files can actually be stored across different areas on your physical disk instead of one continuous stream. For instance imagine you have a 100 unit disk. You save a 20 unit file. You save a 60 unit file. You now delete the first 20 unit file and save a 30 unit file. It will use the first 20 units of space, skip 60, and then use 10 of the last 20 units of space. This is known as fragmentation.

So when you delete a file nothing actually happens to it. Instead its entry in the phone book is changed to 'available'. Now new files in the future can use this space which may happen immediately or months or even years from now depending on a wide array of things. This is how basic 'undelete' software is able to function. This is also for instance why when high security companies want to delete something they ensure that the deleted file is actually overriden multiple times and not simply left as available space.
